doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Mardi Gras, Tremé and passing on New Orleans culture
summary: Marching clubs, neighbourhood musicians, tap dancing like the Nicholas Brothers, Tremé and Preservation Hall shaped her sense of heritage.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: When did you become aware of the heritage and history of your city, or did it make an impression on you that you lived there? Sometimes people who live in a certain area that’s known for something don’t become aware of it as much as those of us that were reading about it from outside.

Let me answer that this way. I became aware of it because of some things that happened in New Orleans, the Mardi Gras. Okay? My parents were in a marching club. So at Mardi Gras they dressed in these costumes and had the band and they marched around. And I grew up with that. And it was understood that this is a part of you, this is a part of what we do, you know, you don’t have to embrace it but you have to be aware of it. Then being around, living in a neighborhood where there were many musicians and you’d hear these guys practicing, you know, you’re sitting on the front porch hearing them practice, you know, playing with their kids and hearing the band practicing in the back yard or something like that. You grew up with that and it was not anything to be — at least I didn’t take it for granted. Because I felt good when I did it. And I can remember even as a child feeling good when I did the music, even to the point where I’d put the turntable on and I’m washing the dishes or something like this, it’s always music. And then I decided that I wanted to do what I saw the Nicholas Brothers do and tapping and getting on the © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

kitchen table and tapping and looking and seeing my father peek around the door. You know and I’m sharing all of these little things with you because that’s how much music was in my life or is in my life now. And as I got older I moved into an area called like the Tremé area of our city where a lot of the music is and where it really came from. You know we have these second lines and the parades and all of this and the people are dancing in the street and all, and then I had the opportunity to go to Preservation Hall and watch all of these older people playing this music. And you start making the connection. If you can see the Humphrey Brothers and all of these guys over here in Preservation Hall and maybe walk six or seven blocks away and see the youngsters doing the same theme, there’s that connection right there. There’s no denying it. There’s no denying what that music is. And the older I get the more important it becomes that I pass this on to youngsters so that they can understand that this is ours, this is a part of our culture. This is what we have brought to America. We’ve brought this to America. We had all of the European music come to us. But we brought this. We brought this out of Congo Square. We brought this from the Dominican Republic. We brought this from all of these places and now you have all of these rhythms going on. You know. And it’s exciting that you’re responding to rhythms and rhythms and rhythms you know. Okay I’m getting excited.
